title: Write SEO-Friendly Content Without Being an SEO Expert
description: Learn how to plan, write, optimize, and improve useful SEO-friendly content without becoming a technical SEO specialist. This practical guide covers search intent, keywords, structure, internal links, images, metadata, and measurement.
content:
# Write SEO-Friendly Content Without Being an SEO Expert

Writing content that performs well in search does not require you to become a full-time SEO technician. You do not need to memorize every ranking-system update, build a complex automation stack, or force the same keyword into every paragraph. What you need is a repeatable editorial process that helps a real reader solve a real problem clearly, completely, and efficiently.

This guide shows you how to create that process. It starts before you write a headline and continues after publication, when you study what readers actually do on the page. The goal is not to write for an algorithm instead of people. The goal is to make genuinely useful content easier for people and search engines to discover, understand, and trust.

![SEO-friendly content workflow showing the path from search intent to useful content, optimization, publication, and improvement](https://smartgentools.com/blog-posts/images/seo-friendly-content-workflow.png)

## What SEO-friendly content really means

SEO-friendly content is content that satisfies a searcher’s purpose while making its subject, scope, and value clear. It has a useful answer, a logical structure, a descriptive title, readable language, helpful links, accessible media, and enough technical clarity for search engines to crawl and interpret the page. It is not content that merely repeats a keyword.

Google’s [SEO Starter Guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide) explains that there are no secret tricks that automatically rank a page first. It emphasizes improvements that help search engines crawl, understand, and serve useful pages. Google’s [Search Essentials](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials) similarly describes people-first content, clear language, crawlable links, and technically accessible pages as foundations rather than shortcuts.

A helpful way to think about SEO is to separate the work into three questions:

| Question | What you are solving | Evidence of a good answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What does the searcher need? | Search intent and the underlying problem | The article answers the main question early and completely |
| How can the reader use the answer? | Clarity, examples, process, and next actions | The content is easy to scan, apply, and remember |
| How can the page be discovered and understood? | Titles, headings, links, images, metadata, and technical access | Search engines can interpret the page and users can find the next useful resource |

When these three questions are answered together, optimization becomes an editing discipline rather than a mysterious technical exercise.

## Step 1: Choose a specific reader and a specific problem

Start with the reader, not the keyword. “SEO content” is a broad topic, but “a small-business owner writing their first service page” describes a person with a concrete situation. Specific readers make better editorial decisions because you can predict what they already know, what may confuse them, and what action they need to take next.

Write a one-sentence problem statement before creating an outline. For example: “A new website owner wants to write useful articles that can appear in search results but does not know how to choose topics, organize a page, or measure improvement.” This sentence becomes a filter for the rest of the article. If a paragraph does not help solve that problem, move it to another article or remove it.

This step also prevents a common failure: creating a page that mentions SEO, content, keywords, tools, and analytics without giving the reader a clear outcome. A focused page can still be comprehensive, but every section should contribute to the reader’s intended result.

## Step 2: Identify the search intent behind the topic

Search intent is the reason someone enters a query. The same subject can produce very different pages depending on what the searcher wants. Someone searching for “what is keyword research” may need a definition. Someone searching for “best keyword research workflow for a small website” may need a comparison and a process. Someone searching for “keyword density checker” may be ready to use a tool.

Before writing, inspect the language and format of pages that already address the topic. You are not copying their content or assuming that current results are perfect. You are looking for clues about the task searchers expect to complete. Are they looking for an explanation, a tutorial, a checklist, a template, a product comparison, or a troubleshooting answer? Your page should meet the dominant need while adding a clear reason to choose it over a shallow alternative.

A simple intent brief can contain the following fields:

| Intent field | Example for this guide |
| --- | --- |
| Main question | How can I write content that is friendly to search engines without being an SEO expert? |
| Reader stage | Beginner who can write but lacks a reliable SEO workflow |
| Desired outcome | A publishable article with a clear structure, useful links, and basic optimization |
| Likely concerns | Keyword stuffing, technical complexity, and uncertainty about measurement |
| Best format | Step-by-step tutorial with examples, templates, and a post-publication review process |

The brief gives you a standard against which you can judge the draft. If the final article turns into an advanced discussion of crawling directives, it may be accurate but still fail the intended reader.

For a deeper foundation, use SmartGen’s guide to [search engine optimization and its core concepts](https://smartgentools.com/blog/search-engine-optimization-seo-the-complete-a-to-z-mega-guide-for-beginners-smartgen-blog/). It provides broader context, while this article focuses on the writing workflow.

## Step 3: Build a small, realistic keyword set

Keywords are words and phrases that describe the subject people search for. They are useful because they reveal language, questions, and distinctions. They are not a script that tells you how many times to repeat a phrase.

Choose one primary phrase that represents the page’s main purpose. Then collect a small group of supporting phrases that represent subtopics, questions, synonyms, and adjacent tasks. For this article, the primary phrase might be “write SEO-friendly content,” while supporting ideas include “search intent,” “content outline,” “internal linking,” “SEO title,” “image alt text,” and “measure content performance.”

A practical keyword set should pass three tests. First, the phrases must describe the same page rather than several unrelated pages. Second, they must be natural enough to use in a sentence. Third, they must help you discover what the reader expects, not merely increase the apparent size of a keyword list.

Do not make keyword density your target. Repetition can make a page awkward and may encourage you to remove useful explanations just to preserve a number. If you want to inspect whether important terms are present and whether a draft has an obvious repetition problem, you can use the [SmartGen Keyword Density Checker](https://smartgentools.com/keyword-density-checker/), but treat its output as an editing clue rather than a ranking formula. Google explicitly warns against keyword stuffing in its SEO guidance.

## Step 4: Design the answer before writing the paragraphs

An outline is where SEO and good writing meet. It helps you cover the important subtopics in a sequence that mirrors the reader’s decision process. Begin with the answer’s promised outcome, then arrange the supporting sections from foundational to practical.

A strong outline for a how-to article usually includes a short introduction, a definition of the problem, a sequence of actions, examples, common mistakes, a measurement section, and a concise conclusion. The outline should not become a collection of disconnected headings. Each section should create a reason to read the next one.

Use headings that communicate the question or task being answered. “Optimize content” is vague. “Write a descriptive title that matches the page’s promise” tells the reader what to do. Headings should be understandable when viewed alone in a table of contents or screen-reader navigation.

A useful test is to remove the paragraphs and read only the headings. Can someone understand the complete route from problem to outcome? If not, the structure needs work before the prose becomes expensive to revise.

## Step 5: Write an opening that confirms relevance quickly

The opening paragraph should reassure the reader that they are in the right place. State the problem, explain the practical outcome, and set a realistic expectation. Avoid beginning with a long history of search engines or a dramatic promise that no article can guarantee.

For example, an effective opening for this guide tells the reader that SEO-friendly writing is a repeatable process, not an advanced technical specialty. It then previews the process: understand intent, create a useful outline, write clearly, optimize the page, add contextual links, and improve it using evidence.

This approach helps users decide whether to continue without hiding the answer behind a long introduction. It also gives search engines and other systems clearer context about the page’s purpose.

## Step 6: Explain the subject completely, but do not add filler

Depth is not the same as length. A long article can still be thin if it repeats general advice without examples, decisions, or evidence. Useful depth comes from answering the follow-up questions a reader will have after each major point.

If you tell readers to “understand search intent,” explain how they can recognize informational, commercial, navigational, and transactional needs. If you recommend “using internal links,” show how to choose a relevant destination and write natural anchor text. If you mention “improving content,” describe what evidence would justify a revision.

Specificity creates value. A good paragraph might explain why a beginner should use one primary topic and a few supporting concepts instead of creating a long list of loosely related keywords. Another paragraph might show how the same topic can require a definition page, a tutorial, or a tool page depending on the searcher’s goal.

Use examples that clarify the method without pretending that one example is a universal rule. Readers should finish a section knowing how to make a similar decision for their own subject.

## Step 7: Place the primary topic naturally

Use the main topic where it improves clarity: in the page title, the opening, a relevant heading, the URL slug, the meta description, and one or more natural body passages. These locations help readers understand the page, but they do not replace useful content.

Use related language when it makes the explanation more precise. A page about SEO-friendly content may naturally discuss search intent, headings, title links, descriptions, crawlable links, images, structured data, and measurement. These concepts are not decorations; they are part of the reader’s task.

Read the draft aloud or use a text-to-speech tool. If the phrase sounds forced, rewrite the sentence. A clear sentence with a natural variation is usually better than an awkward sentence that preserves an exact phrase.

## Step 8: Create a title and description that make an honest promise

The title should describe the page accurately and distinguish it from generic alternatives. It should make the main benefit visible without using exaggerated claims. “How to Write SEO-Friendly Content Without Being an SEO Expert” is useful because it identifies the task and the audience. Adding “A Step-by-Step Guide” makes the format clear.

The meta description is a concise invitation to visit the page. It should summarize what the reader will learn and avoid promising a ranking outcome. Search engines may generate a different snippet when another passage better matches the query, so write a good description for users but do not treat it as a guarantee that every search will display it exactly.

If you need to improve how a title may appear in search results, review the [SmartGen SERP Snippet Preview guide](https://smartgentools.com/blog/google-serp-snippet-preview-tool-the-complete-guide-to-optimizing-your-search-appearance-in-2026/). The tool can help you evaluate clarity and truncation, while the final decision should remain editorial.

## Step 9: Make the page easy to scan and use

Readers often inspect a page before committing to it. Short paragraphs, descriptive headings, examples, tables, and purposeful emphasis help them locate the part they need. Good formatting is not a substitute for substance, but it makes substance easier to use.

Keep one main idea in each paragraph. Follow a general explanation with an example or a decision rule. Use a table when the reader needs to compare options or remember a sequence. Use a list when the items are genuinely parallel; do not turn every paragraph into a list simply because lists look concise.

Mobile readers need particular care. Avoid oversized blocks of text, very wide tables, and images that communicate important information without an accessible text alternative. Preview the page at a narrow width before publishing.

## Step 10: Add contextual internal links that move the reader forward

An internal link is most useful when it answers a related question at the moment the reader is likely to have it. Do not add links merely to increase a count. Link from a meaningful phrase, make the destination’s subject clear, and check that the destination adds value rather than repeating the same introduction.

This guide links to broader SEO fundamentals when a reader needs background, to keyword and snippet resources when the reader needs a practical tool, and to technical pages when the reader is ready for implementation. That creates a topic pathway rather than a random list of URLs.

Use descriptive anchor text. “Read more” tells the reader almost nothing, while “technical SEO optimization guide” communicates the destination. Keep the sentence natural and avoid repeating the exact same anchor phrase every time you link to a page.

A strong internal-linking review asks four questions:

| Review question | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| Is the destination relevant? | It solves a related problem or explains a term used in the current paragraph |
| Is the anchor descriptive? | The linked words indicate what the reader will find |
| Is the link useful now? | It appears where the reader may reasonably need more detail |
| Does the destination work? | The URL resolves, loads on mobile, and is not a duplicate or redirect chain |

For site-wide architecture, compare this process with SmartGen’s [on-page SEO optimization guide](https://smartgentools.com/blog/on-page-seo-optimization-the-complete-a-to-z-mega-guide-for-beginners-smartgen-blog/) and [technical SEO optimization guide](https://smartgentools.com/blog/technical-seo-optimization-the-complete-a-to-z-mega-guide-for-beginners-smartgen-blog/).

## Step 11: Use images as explanations, not decoration

An image should clarify a process, demonstrate a result, or help the reader remember a relationship. Place it close to the paragraph that explains it. Give it descriptive alternative text that communicates its purpose rather than stuffing it with keywords.

The workflow diagram in this article shows the movement from search intent to planning, writing, optimization, publication, and improvement. It is useful because it represents the process described in the text. If the image failed to load, the surrounding paragraphs and alternative text would still communicate the idea.

Use a stable, direct image URL, confirm that the file is served with an image content type, and keep the visual readable on a small screen. Decorative images can use an empty alternative attribute when implemented in HTML, while explanatory images need a concise description.

Google’s SEO guidance recommends placing sharp images near relevant text and writing descriptive alt text. This is an accessibility practice as well as a discoverability practice. It helps people who use screen readers and gives search systems additional context about the visual.

## Step 12: Add basic technical signals without becoming a developer

You do not need to write a crawler to publish a good article, but you should understand the basic checks that protect the reader’s experience. Confirm that the page has a unique title, a readable URL, a useful description, a canonical URL where your platform supports one, and a mobile-friendly layout.

Make sure the page can be reached through normal internal links. A page that exists in a folder but has no navigational path can be difficult for users and crawlers to discover. Confirm that important text is present in the rendered page and not hidden behind an interaction that a search engine or keyboard user cannot use.

Structured data can help a page become eligible for certain search features when it accurately describes the page. It does not guarantee a rich result and should never be used to claim information that is not visible or true. If you want to understand this layer, explore the [SmartGen Schema Markup Generator guide](https://smartgentools.com/blog/free-schema-markup-generator-create-json-ld-structured-data-instantly/).

For broader technical checks, the [SmartGen SEO Audit Tool](https://smartgentools.com/seo-audit-tool/) can help you find common issues. Treat an audit as a diagnostic report. Prioritize problems that affect access, clarity, relevance, or user experience rather than trying to achieve a perfect score at any cost.

## Step 13: Edit for trust, clarity, and original value

Before publishing, revise the article as an editor rather than as a keyword operator. Remove claims you cannot support. Explain unfamiliar terms. Replace vague advice with a method or example. Add a source when a recommendation depends on documented guidance, research, or a changing platform rule.

Show experience where appropriate. A useful article can explain what to do, why it matters, what can go wrong, and how to recognize a good result. If you have tested a workflow, describe the conditions and limitations instead of presenting a personal observation as a universal law.

Check whether the article leaves the reader with a better understanding than the pages they may have already read. If it only restates common definitions, add a template, a decision framework, a worked example, or a troubleshooting section. Original value can come from clarity and application, not only from discovering a new fact.

## Step 14: Publish, inspect, and improve using evidence

Publishing is the beginning of the measurement cycle. Record the article’s publication date, primary topic, intended reader, and target outcome. Then give search systems and readers enough time to produce meaningful signals before changing the page repeatedly.

Look at impressions, clicks, click-through rate, queries, engagement, and conversions in the tools available to you. Interpret each metric in context. High impressions with low clicks may indicate a mismatch between the title and the searcher’s expectation. Clicks with weak engagement may indicate that the opening does not deliver the promised answer. Strong engagement with low impressions may suggest that the page deserves better internal links or broader topic coverage.

Search Console can help you inspect queries and indexing status, while analytics can help you understand what visitors do after arriving. Do not rewrite a page simply because it has not ranked immediately. First check whether it is indexed, whether the intended query matches the page, whether the page is technically accessible, and whether the content provides a strong answer.

Create a simple improvement log. For each revision, record the date, the evidence, the change, and the expected effect. This prevents random edits and helps you learn which improvements actually help your audience.

## A practical pre-publication review

Use this review as a final reading exercise rather than as a mechanical scorecard. A page is ready when it gives a specific reader a complete, honest, and usable answer.

| Area | Question to ask before publishing |
| --- | --- |
| Audience | Is the intended reader and problem clear? |
| Intent | Does the page satisfy the main reason someone would search for this topic? |
| Substance | Does it explain the important decisions, not just name them? |
| Structure | Can a reader understand the route by scanning the headings? |
| Language | Are the main topic and related concepts used naturally? |
| Title and description | Do they make an accurate, compelling promise? |
| Links | Do internal links provide useful next steps and descriptive anchor text? |
| Images | Does every meaningful image have a purpose and useful alt text? |
| Accessibility | Can the page be read and navigated on a small screen and with assistive technology? |
| Technical access | Does the page load, resolve correctly, and remain discoverable through internal navigation? |
| Trust | Are claims accurate, limitations visible, and sources appropriate? |
| Improvement | Do you know which evidence you will review after publication? |

## Common mistakes that make content less SEO-friendly

The first mistake is writing for a keyword instead of a reader. This produces repetitive sentences and often answers a narrower question than the headline suggests. The correction is to define the reader’s problem and use the keyword as a description of that problem, not as a quota.

The second mistake is making the introduction long while delaying the practical answer. Readers should not have to pass through a history lesson before discovering whether the page can help. Put the purpose and outcome near the beginning, then provide context where it helps the decision.

The third mistake is adding internal links without a content relationship. A page filled with unrelated links can feel promotional and can distract from the main task. Link when the destination helps the reader continue, verify, compare, or implement.

The fourth mistake is treating an SEO audit score as the objective. Technical tools are valuable when they reveal a real problem, but a perfect score cannot replace an accurate answer, useful examples, or a page that readers trust. Fix the issues that affect access and usefulness first.

The fifth mistake is publishing once and never learning from the result. Search visibility develops over time, and user behavior can reveal questions that were missing from the first version. A thoughtful update can improve a page more than producing another article on the same subject.

## Final perspective: make the answer worth finding

You do not need to become an SEO expert to write content that search engines can understand and readers want to use. You need to become disciplined about the reader’s problem, the language used to describe it, the structure of the answer, and the evidence you use to improve it.

Start with intent. Build a focused outline. Write a complete answer in natural language. Make the title and headings descriptive. Add internal links that create a useful path. Use images that explain something and alt text that preserves their meaning. Check basic technical access, publish honestly, and improve the page from evidence rather than guesswork.

That process is simple enough for a beginner and strong enough to support a serious content program. Search optimization then becomes what it should have been all along: making valuable information easier for the right people to find.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I write SEO-friendly content without using expensive tools?

Yes. Tools can help you discover questions, inspect technical issues, and measure outcomes, but the foundation is editorial judgment. You can begin with the reader’s problem, a clear outline, careful research, descriptive headings, useful internal links, and a review of the published page. Use tools to reduce uncertainty, not to replace understanding.

### How many keywords should I include in one article?

There is no universal keyword count that makes an article rank. Choose one primary topic and use supporting terms only when they make the explanation more complete or precise. If a phrase makes a sentence unnatural, rewrite the sentence rather than forcing the phrase into it.

### How long should an SEO-friendly article be?

It should be as long as necessary to satisfy the reader’s intent without repeating itself. A short answer can be the best page for a simple question, while a complex tutorial may need examples, decisions, and troubleshooting. Coverage and usefulness matter more than an arbitrary word count.

### Should I update an old article or write a new one?

Update an existing article when it already targets the same intent and can be improved without confusing its purpose. Create a new page when the intent, audience, or promised outcome is meaningfully different. Avoid maintaining several pages that answer the same question with nearly identical content.

### Do internal links guarantee higher rankings?

No. Internal links help users navigate and help search engines discover and understand related pages, but they are not a ranking guarantee. Their value comes from creating a coherent site structure and giving readers relevant next steps.

### What should I measure after publishing?

Start with indexing status, impressions, clicks, click-through rate, queries, engagement, and the action that matters to your website. The right interpretation depends on the page’s purpose. A tutorial may aim for engaged reading and tool usage, while a commercial page may aim for qualified enquiries.

August 14, 2026 • General • By [Sayad Md Bayezid Hosan](https://www.sayadbayezid.com)

# UI/UX Design Course Class 01: Fundamentals

Researchers at Carleton University found that people form a lasting opinion about a website's visual appeal in about **50 milliseconds** — roughly the time it takes to blink. Google later ran its own research and confirmed a similar window, with some judgments forming in as little as 17 milliseconds. That is the entire premise of UI/UX design in one number: before a single word gets read, color, layout, and type have already decided whether someone trusts what they're looking at.

This is Class 01 of the SmartGen UI/UX Design Course, and it covers the four building blocks everything else in this course rests on: what UI/UX design actually is, how color theory works, why color psychology matters (and where it gets oversold), the fundamentals of typography, and the core design principles that tie all of it together.

![UI/UX Design Course Class 01: Fundamentals](https://smartgentools.com/blog-posts/images/ui-ux-design-course-class-01-cover.svg)

---

## Welcome to Class 01 of the SmartGen UI/UX Design Course

This course is built to take you from zero design background to a working, practical understanding of UI/UX design — the kind you can actually apply, not just recognize on a slide. Later classes in this course move into Figma, the UX research process, applied app and web design projects, and eventually building a portfolio and finding freelance work. None of that holds up without the fundamentals in this class first. A beautifully laid-out Figma file built on poor color contrast and inconsistent type still fails the person using it.

So before touching any design software, this class stays entirely conceptual — and deliberately so. Every principle here transfers to every tool you'll ever use, while software interfaces change every few years.

---

## 1. What Is UI/UX Design?

**UI (User Interface)** is everything a person sees and directly interacts with: buttons, colors, icons, spacing, typography, the layout of a screen. **UX (User Experience)** is the entire journey a person has with a product — how easy it is to find what they need, how it makes them feel, whether it does what they expected, and whether they'd come back.

A useful way to separate the two: **UI is what it looks like. UX is how it works.**

### Why the Two Can't Really Be Separated

Picture a checkout button that's perfectly styled — right color, right size, nice shadow, sits exactly where a designer intended. That's good UI. Now picture that same button buried three scrolls down a page, after a confusing form with no indication of what step you're on. The UI is excellent. The UX has failed completely, and the sale is lost anyway.

The reverse happens just as often. A product can have flawless information architecture and a genuinely intuitive flow, but if the interface uses low-contrast gray text on a white background, or uses five different fonts with no clear hierarchy, users will still struggle — not because the *experience* was designed badly, but because the *interface* is actively working against it.

Good products need both working in the same direction. That's the entire reason this class treats color, psychology, typography, and principles as one connected topic instead of four separate ones.

### Related Roles You'll Hear Mentioned

As you go further into design work — especially once freelancing comes up later in this course — you'll see these titles used somewhat interchangeably, though they lean toward different parts of the process:

- **UI Designer** — focuses primarily on visual design: color, typography, layout, component design.
- **UX Designer** — focuses primarily on research, flows, information architecture, and usability testing.
- **UX Researcher** — focuses specifically on understanding user behavior through interviews, testing, and data.
- **Product Designer** — a broader title that typically covers both UI and UX, often with more involvement in business and product strategy.

At smaller companies and in most freelance work, one person often wears all four hats — which is exactly why this course builds the fundamentals for all of them before specializing.

---

## 2. Color Theory: The Designer's Foundation

Color is the first thing anyone perceives about a design, often before they've consciously registered layout or text. Color theory is simply the structured, learnable system behind what makes color combinations feel balanced instead of accidental.

### The Color Wheel

The traditional color wheel organizes color into three tiers:

- **Primary colors** — red, yellow, and blue. These can't be created by mixing other colors.
- **Secondary colors** — orange, green, and purple. Each is made by mixing two primary colors.
- **Tertiary colors** — colors like red-orange or blue-green, made by mixing a primary with a neighboring secondary.

Digital designers rarely mix paint, but the wheel still matters because it's the map every color harmony below is built from.

### Building Color Harmonies

A "harmony" is simply a formula for picking colors that work together, based on their position on the wheel.

| Harmony Type | How It Works | Best Used For |
|---|---|---|
| **Complementary** | Two colors directly opposite each other (blue & orange) | High-contrast call-to-action buttons, energetic brands |
| **Analogous** | Three colors sitting next to each other (blue, teal, green) | Calm, cohesive interfaces — wellness and finance apps |
| **Triadic** | Three colors evenly spaced around the wheel | Playful, vibrant products — kids' apps, entertainment |
| **Split-Complementary** | A base color plus the two colors beside its complement | Bold contrast with slightly more balance than pure complementary |
| **Monochromatic** | Different tints and shades of a single hue | Minimal, elegant dashboards and corporate tools |

None of these is objectively "better" — the right harmony depends entirely on what the product needs to communicate. A meditation app reaching for a triadic red-yellow-blue scheme would fight against its own purpose.

### Warm vs. Cool Colors

Reds, oranges, and yellows are **warm** — they tend to feel energetic, urgent, or inviting, and they visually advance toward the viewer. Blues, greens, and purples are **cool** — they tend to feel calm, trustworthy, or professional, and they visually recede. Most real interfaces mix both: a cool, neutral base (blues and grays) with one warm accent color reserved specifically for the action you most want someone to take.

### How Designers Actually Work With Color on Screens

Print design uses CMYK. Screens don't. As a UI/UX designer, you'll work almost exclusively in three formats:

- **HEX** — a six-character code like `#3B82F6`, the most common format in design tools and CSS.
- **RGB** — Red, Green, Blue values from 0–255 each, e.g. `rgb(59, 130, 246)`.
- **HSL** — Hue, Saturation, Lightness, e.g. `hsl(217, 91%, 60%)`. This format is often the easiest to reason about, since adjusting lightness alone gives you an instant tint or shade of the same color without guessing new HEX values.

If you want to pull a color palette directly from a photo or a piece of inspiration you've found, the [SmartGen Color Palette Extractor](https://smartgentools.com/color-palette-extractor/) does this instantly — upload an image and it returns the dominant HEX codes so you can build a coherent palette from something you're already drawn to, rather than guessing.

### The 60-30-10 Rule

This is the single most practical color rule in UI design: **60% of your interface should use a dominant, usually neutral color** (backgrounds, large surfaces), **30% a secondary color** (supporting elements, secondary buttons, headers), **and 10% an accent color** reserved almost exclusively for the action you want users to notice — usually your primary call-to-action button. Interfaces that ignore this ratio tend to either feel visually flat (too much of one neutral color) or overwhelming (too many competing colors fighting for attention at once).

If you want to test how a full color scheme feels together before committing, the [SmartGen Color Schemes tool](https://smartgentools.com/html-code-library/color-codes/color-schemes/) and [HTML Color Picker](https://smartgentools.com/html-code-library/color-codes/html-color-picker/) are both useful for previewing combinations against the 60-30-10 split described above.

### Where Color Meets Accessibility

Color choice isn't purely aesthetic — it has a hard technical floor. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) require a **minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1** between text and its background for normal-sized text, and **3:1** for large text and interactive UI components, to meet Level AA compliance — the baseline most legal and industry standards are built around. This isn't a minor detail: research from WebAIM's ongoing accessibility audits has found that **contrast failures appear in over 80% of websites tested**, making it the single most common accessibility violation on the web. We'll come back to exactly why this matters in Section 5.

---

## 3. Color Psychology: Why Colors Make Us Feel Things

Color psychology is the study of how color influences perception and emotion. It's genuinely useful — and also one of the most oversimplified topics in design content online, so it's worth covering carefully rather than handing you a chart and calling it science.

### Common Color Associations in Western Design

The table below reflects patterns that show up consistently across Western commercial design — not universal laws of human perception.

| Color | Common Association | Frequently Seen In |
|---|---|---|
| **Red** | Urgency, passion, appetite, danger | Sale banners, error states, food delivery apps |
| **Blue** | Trust, calm, stability, professionalism | Banking apps, social platforms, healthcare |
| **Green** | Growth, health, "go" / success | Financial gains, eco-friendly brands, confirmations |
| **Yellow** | Optimism, energy, caution | Warning states, youthful or playful brands |
| **Purple** | Creativity, luxury, imagination | Beauty brands, creative tools, premium tiers |
| **Black** | Sophistication, authority, premium | Luxury goods, high-end technology |
| **White** | Simplicity, cleanliness, openness | Minimalist apps, healthcare, Apple-style interfaces |

### The Important Caveat: Context and Culture Change Everything

This is the part most beginner design content skips. Color meaning is not fixed or universal — it shifts by culture, industry, and individual experience. White reads as purity and simplicity in most Western design, but represents mourning in several East Asian cultures. Red signals danger and "stop" across most of the West, but represents luck and celebration throughout much of Chinese culture. Even within one culture, context overrides convention constantly — red means "error" in a form field, but the exact same red means "sale, buy now" on an e-commerce banner two inches away.

The honest takeaway: treat color psychology as a reasonable starting hypothesis, not a settled rule. Test real color choices against your actual audience whenever the stakes are high enough to justify it, rather than assuming a chart from a blog post applies universally.

### Designing for Colorblind Users

This is where color psychology and accessibility intersect directly. Color vision deficiency affects roughly **8% of men and 0.5% of women worldwide** — around 300 million people globally — with red-green color blindness accounting for about 99% of cases. That means in any reasonably sized user base, a meaningful slice of your audience physically cannot distinguish the "urgent red" from the "confirmed green" your color psychology chart promised would communicate two opposite things.

The practical rule that follows: **never use color as the only signal for meaning.** An error state should pair red with an icon and text, not red alone. A "success" state needs a checkmark, not just a green background. This single habit prevents an entire category of accessibility failures before they happen.

---

## 4. Typography: Giving Your Interface a Voice

If color sets the mood, typography carries the actual content — and it does more of the communicative work than most beginners initially assume.

### Font Categories

- **Serif** — fonts with small decorative strokes at the ends of letters (like Georgia or Times New Roman). They tend to read as traditional, editorial, or trustworthy.
- **Sans-serif** — fonts without those strokes (like Inter, Helvetica, or Roboto). They read as clean, modern, and are the dominant choice for digital interfaces because they render clearly at small sizes on screens.
- **Monospace** — every character occupies equal width (like Fira Code or Courier). Used almost exclusively for code, technical data, or anything that needs to align in columns.
- **Display / Decorative** — expressive, stylized fonts meant for large headlines only. They break down and become unreadable at body-text sizes.

### Building a Type Hierarchy

Typography creates order through deliberate contrast in size, weight, and spacing — not through arbitrary variation. A typical hierarchy moves from a large, bold headline (H1) down through progressively smaller subheadings (H2, H3) to a comfortably sized, lighter-weight body text, with captions or metadata smaller still. This hierarchy is what lets someone scan a screen in two seconds and immediately know what matters most, without reading every word — the same principle behind why this article uses headings the way it does.

### Readability Rules That Actually Matter

- **Line length:** aim for roughly **50–75 characters per line**. Shorter lines force the eye to jump too often; longer lines make it easy to lose your place returning to the start of the next line.
- **Line height (leading):** set line height around **1.4–1.6× the font size**. Text set too tight feels cramped and fatiguing to read; too loose and lines feel disconnected from each other.
- **Minimum size:** body text on the web should generally sit at **16px or larger**. Smaller sizes push accessibility problems onto users with any degree of visual impairment — which, combined with age-related vision changes, is a substantial share of any general audience.

### Pairing Fonts Without Making a Mess

The safest, most reliable rule for beginners: **limit any single interface to two or three fonts total** — often just one, used at different weights and sizes. When pairing two, choose fonts with clear contrast in personality (a distinctive display font for headlines, paired with a neutral, highly readable sans-serif for body text) rather than two fonts that are almost — but not quite — the same, which reads as a mistake rather than a choice.

### Typography Meets Accessibility

Beyond size, avoid setting long passages of body text in **all caps** — it removes the natural shape cues (ascenders and descenders) that make words fast to recognize, slowing reading speed measurably. And exactly like color, typography needs sufficient contrast against its background — a beautifully chosen font in light gray on white fails the same 4.5:1 contrast requirement covered in the next section, regardless of how good the font choice itself is.

---

## 5. Core UI/UX Design Principles

This section is where color, psychology, and typography stop being separate topics and become one connected design practice. These principles apply regardless of what you're designing — a mobile app, a dashboard, or a landing page you'll build in later classes.

### Visual Hierarchy

Visual hierarchy is the deliberate use of size, color, contrast, and position to guide the eye to what matters most, first. Every screen should have one clear focal point — usually the primary action you want a user to take — with everything else supporting, not competing with, that focal point.

### Consistency

The same element should look and behave the same way everywhere it appears. If a "Save" button is blue and rounded on one screen, it shouldn't become green and square on the next. Consistency is what lets users build a mental model of how a product works, so they stop having to relearn it on every screen.

### Contrast & Accessibility

This is where Section 2's WCAG numbers become an active design principle, not just a technical footnote. Every meaningful text-to-background pairing needs to hit **4.5:1** for normal text and **3:1** for large text and UI components (like button borders and icons) to meet WCAG 2.1/2.2 Level AA — the standard most accessibility audits and legal requirements are measured against today. WCAG 3.0 is still a working draft as of 2026, expected to eventually introduce a more nuanced contrast algorithm — but 2.1/2.2 AA remains the practical bar to design against right now.

### Feedback & Affordance

**Affordance** means an element visually suggests how it should be used — a button should look pressable, a toggle should look toggleable. **Feedback** means the interface responds every time a user takes an action — a button changes state when clicked, a form shows a clear success or error message, a loading state appears while something processes. Interfaces that go silent after an action leave users unsure whether anything happened at all, which is one of the fastest ways to erode trust in a product.

### Simplicity and Cognitive Load

**Hick's Law** — a well-established finding in human-computer interaction — states that the time it takes someone to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices available. In practice: every unnecessary button, option, or piece of text on a screen adds a small tax to how quickly someone can act. Good design constantly asks what can be removed, not just what can be added.

### White Space

Empty space isn't wasted space — it's what makes everything else on a screen legible and calm rather than cramped and chaotic. Generous spacing around text and elements consistently reads as more premium, more trustworthy, and easier to scan, even though nothing about the actual content has changed.

### Grounded in a Real Framework: Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics

These six principles aren't invented for this course — they align closely with **Jakob Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics**, first published in 1994 through the Nielsen Norman Group and still the most widely cited usability framework in the industry today.

| # | Heuristic | What It Means in Practice |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Visibility of system status | Always show users what's happening — loaders, progress, confirmations |
| 2 | Match between system and the real world | Use familiar language and concepts, not internal jargon |
| 3 | User control and freedom | Always provide an obvious way to undo or go back |
| 4 | Consistency and standards | The same element should behave the same way everywhere |
| 5 | Error prevention | Design so mistakes are hard to make in the first place |
| 6 | Recognition rather than recall | Show options; don't make users remember them |
| 7 | Flexibility and efficiency of use | Support shortcuts for experienced users without cluttering things for beginners |
| 8 | Aesthetic and minimalist design | Remove anything that doesn't serve the content or the task |
| 9 | Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors | Plain-language error messages that suggest a fix |
| 10 | Help and documentation | Make help easy to find, searchable, and task-focused |

You don't need to memorize this list today — but recognizing it will make every later class in this course, and every design critique you ever receive, make a lot more sense.

---

## Common Mistakes Beginners Make

- **Picking colors because they look nice, without testing contrast.** A palette can be visually appealing and still fail WCAG AA — always check, don't assume.
- **Using more than two or three fonts in one design.** Almost always reads as inconsistent rather than expressive.
- **Relying on color alone to communicate status.** Pair every red/green/yellow state with an icon or text label too.
- **Ignoring line length and line height.** Beautiful typography set too tight or too wide still fails to be readable.
- **Copying a color psychology chart literally.** Treat it as a hypothesis to test against your actual audience, not a guarantee.
- **Designing with no white space.** Cramming more in rarely communicates more — it usually communicates less, more slowly.
- **Only checking designs at desktop size.** A font size or contrast ratio that works on a large monitor can fail completely on a small phone screen in daylight.

---

## Practice: Your First Design Audit

You don't need any design software to start applying this class — just three apps or websites you already use regularly. For each one, spend five minutes answering:

1. **Colors:** What's the dominant color (60%)? The secondary color (30%)? What single accent color (10%) is used for the main action button? (The [SmartGen HTML Color Picker](https://smartgentools.com/html-code-library/color-codes/html-color-picker/) can help you pull exact HEX values if you're inspecting screenshots.)
2. **Typography:** How many distinct fonts can you spot? Is there a clear size/weight hierarchy between headings and body text?
3. **Hierarchy:** What's the very first thing your eye lands on on the main screen? Is that the same thing the product most wants you to do?
4. **Accessibility:** Can you find any text that feels hard to read against its background? Would it likely pass a 4.5:1 contrast check?

This exercise trains the single most valuable habit in design: noticing deliberate choices in products you already trust, instead of only critiquing your own work in isolation.

---

## Knowledge Check

**1. What's the core difference between UI and UX?**
UI is what a product looks like and the elements a user directly interacts with. UX is the entire experience of using the product — how easy, intuitive, and satisfying that journey feels.

**2. Name three of the five color harmony types covered in this class.**
Any three of: complementary, analogous, triadic, split-complementary, monochromatic.

**3. What WCAG AA contrast ratio is required for normal body text?**
4.5:1 (with 3:1 for large text and UI components).

**4. True or false: color psychology means the same color triggers the same emotion in every culture.**
False. Color associations shift significantly by culture, industry, and context — they're a starting hypothesis, not a universal rule.

**5. Why does limiting a design to two or three fonts usually produce a better result?**
More than that tends to read as inconsistent or accidental rather than intentional, and it works against the hierarchy that helps users scan a screen quickly.

---

## Visual Summary

The infographic below maps all five fundamentals covered in this class — including a working color wheel and the 60-30-10 color distribution rule — as a single visual reference.

![UI/UX Design Fundamentals infographic — color theory, color psychology, typography, and design principles](https://smartgentools.com/blog-posts/images/ui-ux-design-course-class-01-infographic.svg)

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What's the difference between UI design and UX design?**
UI (User Interface) design covers the visual and interactive elements a person sees and touches — buttons, color, typography, layout. UX (User Experience) design covers the entire journey someone has with a product, including usability, flow, and how it makes them feel. Most real design work involves both together.

**Do I need to know how to code to learn UI/UX design?**
No. UI/UX design and front-end development are related but separate skills. Understanding basic HTML/CSS concepts (like how HEX colors work, covered in this class) helps you communicate with developers, but it isn't a requirement to design well.

**What's the best color scheme for a beginner to start with?**
Start with a monochromatic or analogous scheme using the 60-30-10 rule from Section 2 — it's the hardest combination to get visually wrong, and it teaches restraint before you move on to bolder complementary or triadic palettes.

**Is color psychology backed by real science?**
Partially, and with real limits. There's genuine research behind broad tendencies (warm colors reading as more urgent, for example), but color psychology is far more context- and culture-dependent than most infographics suggest. Treat it as a starting point to test, not a rule to follow blindly.

**How many fonts should I use in one design?**
Two to three at most, and often just one font used at different weights and sizes is enough. More than that usually reads as inconsistent rather than intentional.

**What is WCAG and why does it matter for designers, not just developers?**
WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the standard framework for making digital content usable by people with disabilities, including visual impairments and color blindness. Contrast ratio — a direct design decision, not a coding one — is one of its most common failure points, which is why it belongs in a design fundamentals class, not just a developer's checklist.

**Do I need Figma to follow this course?**
Not for this class. Class 01 is entirely conceptual by design, so the principles transfer to any tool. Figma setup begins in Module 2.

**What's the difference between UI/UX design and graphic design?**
Graphic design is typically static and one-directional — posters, logos, print materials. UI/UX design is interactive and system-based — it has to account for different screen sizes, user states (loading, error, success), and how a person actually behaves when using it, not just how it looks in a single frame.

**How long does it take to learn UI/UX design fundamentals?**
The concepts in this class can be understood in a single sitting, but recognizing them consistently in real products — the goal of the practice exercise above — is a habit that builds over weeks, not hours. Give yourself time to notice these patterns in apps you already use before moving to Module 2.

**What should I learn after color, typography, and design principles?**
Module 2 of this course moves into Figma — the industry-standard design tool — starting with its interface, then components, auto layout, and building your first design system, which is where these fundamentals get applied directly.

---

content: # Adsterra Review and Publisher Guide: The Complete A-to-Z Walkthrough for Bloggers *Disclosure: this guide includes Adsterra referral links and official Adsterra promotional banners. Signing up through them costs you nothing extra and helps support this site — the comparison and advice below are the same either way.* If you run a blog, a tool site, or any kind of content platform and you're looking for ways to earn from your traffic, two names come up constantly: Google AdSense and Adsterra. This guide walks through what Adsterra actually is, how it honestly compares to AdSense, and exactly how to get started — including the parts most promotional pages leave out. ## What Is Adsterra? Adsterra is a global advertising network founded in 2013, connecting a large base of publishers (site owners who want to run ads) with advertisers who want to reach their traffic. It's grown into one of the larger self-serve ad networks in the industry, working with tens of thousands of direct publishers across a wide range of ad formats and payout models. For publishers, it works the way most ad networks do: you sign up, add your site, get approved, paste a small piece of ad code onto your pages, and get paid based on how many people see or interact with the ads — depending on which pricing model your ad units use. ## Why Beginners Look at Adsterra Before (or Alongside) AdSense This is the honest reason Adsterra shows up in nearly every "how to monetize your blog" conversation: **Google AdSense has a real approval bar.** It wants original content, reasonable traffic, and full policy compliance — and it rejects a lot of new sites, sometimes more than once, before accepting them. Adsterra's approval process is dramatically more lenient. There's no minimum traffic requirement, and approval is often close to instant. That makes it a genuinely reasonable option if you're publishing consistently but haven't been accepted into AdSense yet, or if a meaningful share of your traffic comes from regions where AdSense's own fill rate and CPM tend to be weaker. Worth being upfront about before you get excited: publisher discussions and independent comparisons consistently note that AdSense generally pays more per thousand views once you're eligible for it. Adsterra is best understood as a strong "start earning right now" option and a useful supplement — not necessarily a permanent replacement if AdSense is realistically within reach for your site. ## Adsterra vs Google AdSense: The Honest Comparison | | Adsterra | Google AdSense | |---|---|---| | **Approval** | Often instant, typically within 24 hours | Manual review; commonly days to weeks, multiple rejections are common for new sites | | **Traffic minimum** | None | None officially, but low-traffic sites are frequently rejected in practice | | **Ad formats** | Popunder, Social Bar, In-Page Push, Native, Banner, Direct Link, Interstitial | Display banner, native, in-feed, in-article, matched content | | **Typical CPM** | Generally lower, varies heavily by GEO and format | Generally higher, especially for Tier-1 (US/UK/CA/AU) traffic | | **Minimum payout** | As low as $5, depending on payment method | $100 | | **Payout frequency** | Weekly for established accounts, after an initial hold | Monthly | | **Best for** | New sites, global/Tier-2-3 traffic, testing monetization fast | Established sites with quality traffic, especially Tier-1 | Neither column is the universally "correct" choice — they solve different problems at different stages of a site's life, which is exactly why a lot of publishers end up running both. ## The Ad Formats Adsterra Offers — and Which Ones to Actually Use Adsterra gives publishers more format variety than AdSense does, but not all of them are equally friendly to your readers or to running alongside AdSense cleanly: - **Banner ads** — standard display units. Low-risk, familiar to readers, safe to run anywhere. - **Native ads** — styled to blend with your site's content. Generally unobtrusive. - **Social Bar** — an interactive notification-style format. Reasonably contained if placed carefully. - **In-Page Push** — simulates a push notification within the page. More attention-grabbing than a banner. - **Direct Links** — a link that sends a visitor to an advertiser's page when clicked, with no visible ad unit until it's clicked. - **Popunder** — opens a new browser window or tab behind the current one. Historically one of Adsterra's highest-earning formats, and also the one that generates the most reader complaints when overused. - **Interstitial** — a full-page ad shown between content views. The honest recommendation: **if you're also running AdSense, or you simply care about reader trust, lead with Banner, Native, and Social Bar.** Google's own AdSense placement policy explicitly prohibits ads delivered as pop-ups, so running Popunders on pages that also carry AdSense is a real risk to your AdSense standing, not just a UX nitpick. If you want to test Popunder or Interstitial for the extra revenue, keep them isolated to pages or sections that don't run AdSense at all. ## Step-by-Step: Signing Up and Adding the Code Signing up costs nothing — Adsterra doesn't charge publishers to join. 1. **Create your account.** Sign up through [this Adsterra referral link](https://beta.publishers.adsterra.com/referral/jcz6DrZ9pY) and select "Publisher" during registration. 2. **Add your website.** Enter your domain and basic details about your content and traffic. 3. **Wait for review.** Approval is frequently instant and rarely takes more than 24 hours for a normal, policy-compliant site — no waiting weeks like a first-time AdSense application often involves. 4. **Pick your ad format(s).** Start with Banner or Native for the safest option, based on the placement guidance above. 5. **Copy your ad code.** Adsterra generates a small JavaScript snippet for each ad unit you create in the dashboard. 6. **Paste the code into your site.** On WordPress, this usually means a header/footer script plugin, a widget area, or directly into your theme's template, depending on where you want the unit to appear. 7. **Confirm it's live.** Check the page — ideally in a private/incognito browser window, since ad networks don't always serve test ads to your own logged-in session — to confirm the unit is actually rendering. That's the entire technical lift: no coding beyond pasting a snippet where you want the ad to appear. ## The Honest Pros and Cons **What Adsterra genuinely does well:** - Fast, low-barrier approval with no traffic minimum — a real, verified advantage for new sites - Multiple payout methods with a low minimum threshold - Weekly payouts once your account is established, versus AdSense's monthly cycle - Strong fill rates for global and Tier-2/Tier-3 traffic that AdSense often monetizes weakly - An established company — it's been operating since 2013, not a fly-by-night operation **What to know before you commit:** - CPM is generally lower than AdSense for comparable Tier-1 traffic — set expectations accordingly - The higher-earning formats (Popunder, Interstitial) are intrusive enough to hurt reader experience if overused, and can conflict with AdSense's own placement rules - Publisher reviews on independent platforms show a recurring pattern of complaints about withheld balances or account suspensions — this isn't unique to Adsterra among networks in this tier, but it's real enough that you should read the terms of service carefully, keep your own records, and avoid treating any single ad network as your only income stream - Payout experience can vary by account manager, GEO, and niche — one publisher's report isn't a guarantee of what you'll see **Who might want to skip it, at least for now:** if your site already has approved, healthy AdSense revenue from mostly Tier-1 traffic, the added complexity of a second network may not be worth the marginal revenue. Adsterra earns its place mainly for sites that can't get AdSense yet, or that have meaningful traffic AdSense doesn't monetize well. ## Running Adsterra and AdSense Together, Safely Google explicitly permits non-Google ad networks on the same site or page as AdSense — this isn't a gray area, it's stated directly in Google's own publisher documentation. Two things actually matter for staying compliant: 1. **Ad density.** Your content needs to outweigh your ads on the page — don't stack multiple large ad units on top of each other. 2. **Placement rules.** No ads that encourage accidental clicks, no misleading labels, and critically, no ads delivered as pop-ups on any page carrying AdSense — exactly why the format guidance above steers you toward Banner, Native, and Social Bar on those pages. Handled that way, running both is a common, unremarkable setup. Many publishers run AdSense on their main content and lean on Adsterra's other formats to monetize the traffic AdSense fills poorly. If you're also working on the content and traffic side — really the bigger lever for either network's earnings — [our SEO guide](https://smartgentools.com/blog/search-engine-optimization-seo-the-complete-a-to-z-mega-guide-for-beginners-smartgen-blog/) covers how to grow the traffic you're now trying to monetize. ## Other Networks Worth Knowing About Adsterra isn't the only option in this space, and a genuinely complete picture includes knowing that. Names that come up alongside it in independent comparisons include PropellerAds (a similarly broad, low-barrier network), Media.net (contextual ads, closer in style to AdSense), and Ezoic (an AI-driven layout/optimization layer that can sit on top of your existing ad setup). None of them change the core trade-off in this guide — low barrier to entry versus typically lower CPM than AdSense — but it's worth knowing Adsterra is one reasonable option among several, not the only one. ## Get Started With Adsterra Sign-up is free, and approval is usually fast. **[Join Adsterra as a publisher →](https://beta.publishers.adsterra.com/referral/jcz6DrZ9pY)** *Sidebar-sized banner — place this in a sidebar or widget area rather than in body text, since 160×600 is a tall skyscraper format, not an inline one:* ## Frequently Asked Questions **Is Adsterra free to join?** Yes. There's no cost to sign up or to add ad code to your site as a publisher. **Do I need a minimum amount of traffic?** No. Adsterra has no stated traffic minimum, which is the main reason it's popular with new sites that don't yet qualify for AdSense. **How fast is approval?** Commonly within 24 hours, and often close to instant for a normal, policy-compliant site. **Can I use Adsterra and AdSense on the same website?** Yes — Google explicitly allows non-Google ad networks alongside AdSense, as long as you follow AdSense's ad density and placement rules, in particular avoiding pop-up-style formats on any page that also runs AdSense. **Which ad format should I start with?** Banner or Native, if you want the format least likely to annoy readers or conflict with AdSense. Popunders and Interstitials generally pay more per impression but are more intrusive. **How and when do I get paid?** Adsterra supports multiple payment methods with a minimum payout as low as $5 depending on the method, moving to weekly payouts once your account is established. **Should I drop AdSense once I'm approved, and just use Adsterra?** Generally no — AdSense typically pays more for the traffic it monetizes well. The more common, more profitable setup is running both, with AdSense on your main content and Adsterra's gentler formats filling in elsewhere. ## Conclusion Adsterra isn't a replacement for AdSense, and it isn't trying to be one — it's a fast, low-barrier way to start earning from a site AdSense hasn't accepted yet, or to pick up revenue from traffic AdSense doesn't monetize well. Used with the placement guidance above, it's a reasonable, honest addition to a blog's monetization stack. The referral link and banners in this guide are how you can support this site if you decide to give it a try — but the comparison above holds either way. --- *Written for the SmartGen Tools blog by Sayad Md Bayezid Hosan.* --- --- * [Related Article 1](https://smartgentools.com/blog/search-engine-optimization-seo-the-complete-a-to-z-mega-guide-for-beginners-smartgen-blog/) * [Related Article 2](https://smartgentools.com/blog/how-to-do-keyword-research-for-seo-complete-guide/)
