## General Questions

### What is SmartGen Docs?

SmartGen Docs is a lightweight, open-source static site generator designed to help you create professional and responsive documentation websites from Markdown files. It focuses on simplicity, speed, and ease of deployment.

### Is SmartGen Docs free to use?

Yes, SmartGen Docs is open-source and completely free to use under the [MIT License](https://docs.smartgentools.com/about/license.md).

### What are the main benefits of using SmartGen Docs?

Key benefits include:

- **Simplicity**: Easy to learn and use, especially for those familiar with Markdown.
- **Speed**: Generates static HTML, resulting in fast-loading websites.
- **Flexibility**: Customizable themes and a clear project structure.
- **Open Source**: Community-driven development and transparent codebase.
- **Deployment**: Easy deployment to various static site hosting platforms like GitHub Pages, Netlify, and Vercel.

### What are the system requirements for SmartGen Docs?

SmartGen Docs requires Python 3.8 or newer and `pip` for installation. No other specific system requirements are typically needed beyond a standard development environment.

## Installation and Setup

### How do I install SmartGen Docs?

You can install SmartGen Docs using `pip`:

```
pip install smartgen-docs
Copy
```

For detailed instructions, refer to the [Installation Guide](https://docs.smartgentools.com/getting-started/installation.md).

To upgrade, use the following `pip` command:

```
pip install --upgrade smartgen-docs
Copy
```

This usually indicates that the Python scripts directory is not in your system's PATH. Ensure that `pip`'s installation directory is included in your system's PATH environment variable. You might need to restart your terminal after installation.

Yes, SmartGen Docs supports customizable themes using Jinja2 templates. You can modify existing themes or create your own. Refer to the [Customization Guide](https://docs.smartgentools.com/guides/customization.md) for more information.

All your Markdown source files (`.md`) should be placed within the `docs/` directory of your project. You can create subdirectories within `docs/` to organize your content logically.

### How do I add a new page to my documentation?

1. Create a new Markdown file (e.g., `docs/my-new-page.md`).
2. Add the new page to the `nav` section of your `smartgen.yml` file to make it appear in the navigation menu. For example:



```
nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - My New Page: my-new-page.md
Copy
```

### How do I create nested navigation menus?

You can create nested menus in your `smartgen.yml` by defining a dictionary where the key is the parent menu item and the value is a list of its child pages. For example:

      - Child Page 1: parent-section/child-page-1.md

# How to Do Keyword Research for SEO: The Complete Step-by-Step Guide

Ahrefs' own data puts it bluntly: roughly **90% of content gets zero traffic from Google**. The single biggest reason isn't bad writing — it's that the keyword was never worth targeting in the first place. Either nobody searches for it, it's impossibly competitive, or it doesn't actually match what the searcher wanted.

Keyword research is the process that prevents that outcome. Done properly, it tells you exactly what your audience is typing into Google, how many of them are typing it, how hard it will be to rank for, and — most importantly — whether ranking for it would actually be worth anything to your business.

This guide walks through the complete picture: the different types of keywords you'll encounter, every major metric used to evaluate them, why "zero volume" doesn't mean zero opportunity, why long-tail keywords deserve more attention than most beginners give them, and a practical, step-by-step framework for deciding what to actually prioritize.

## What You'll Learn in This Guide

- [Types of Keywords](#types-of-keywords)
- [Keyword SEO Metrics Explained](#keyword-metrics-explained)
- [Traffic Potential](#traffic-potential)
- ["Zero-Volume" Keywords](#zero-volume-keywords)
- [Long-Tail Keywords](#long-tail-keywords)
- [Business Potential Score](#business-potential-score)
- [High-Volume Keywords](#high-volume-keywords)
- [How to Prioritize Keywords](#how-to-prioritize-keywords)
- [Step-by-Step Keyword Research Process](#step-by-step-process)
- [Frequently Asked Questions](#faq)

---

## Types of Keywords {#types-of-keywords}

Before touching any metric, it helps to know what you're actually looking at. Keywords aren't one category — they fall into several distinct types, and mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

**Short-tail (head) keywords** — One or two words, extremely broad, and enormous search volume. "Shoes" or "SEO" are head terms. They're the hardest to rank for and often the vaguest in terms of what the searcher actually wants.

**Long-tail keywords** — Three or more words, highly specific, lower individual volume, but far easier to rank for and much more likely to convert. Covered in full depth in its own section below.

**Informational keywords** — The searcher wants to learn something. "How does keyword difficulty work" or "what is CPC in SEO." These usually map to blog posts, guides, and tutorials.

**Navigational keywords** — The searcher already knows where they want to go and is using Google as a shortcut. "Gmail login" or "SmartGen tools" are navigational.

**Commercial investigation keywords** — The searcher is comparing options before buying. "Best keyword research tools" or "Ahrefs vs Semrush" fall here — not ready to buy yet, but close.

**Transactional keywords** — The searcher is ready to act right now. "Buy keyword research tool," "SEO agency pricing," or "sign up for [tool] free trial."

**Branded vs. non-branded keywords** — A branded keyword includes a company or product name ("SmartGen SEO tools"). A non-branded keyword describes the need without naming a specific brand ("free SEO tools online"). Non-branded keywords are almost always the priority for new sites, since branded search only exists once people already know you.

**Local keywords** — Tied to a specific geographic area, such as "SEO agency in Dhaka" or "plumber near me." If your business serves a specific location, local keywords deserve dedicated attention — our [Local SEO and Google Business Profile guide](https://smartgentools.com/blog/local-seo-and-google-business-profile-the-complete-a-to-z-mega-guide-for-beginners-smartgen-blog/) covers this in full depth.

Most real keyword lists are a mix of several of these types at once. A single keyword can be simultaneously long-tail, non-branded, and commercial investigation — the categories aren't mutually exclusive, and the more of them you can identify in a single keyword, the clearer picture you get of what content will actually satisfy it.

---

## Keyword SEO Metrics Explained {#keyword-metrics-explained}

Knowing what a keyword *is* only gets you halfway. To decide whether it's actually worth targeting, you need to read the metrics correctly — and just as importantly, know where each metric falls short. Every major keyword research tool (Ahrefs, Semrush, Google Keyword Planner, Ubersuggest) surfaces some version of the following seven metrics.

### Search Volume

The estimated average number of monthly searches for a keyword in a given location. This is the number most beginners look at first — and lean on far too heavily. A keyword's search volume tells you *demand*, but says nothing about how much of that traffic you'd actually capture, since first-page results, paid ads, and — increasingly — AI-generated answers all split that demand before it ever reaches your site.

### Keyword Difficulty (KD)

A 0–100 score estimating how hard it would be to rank in the top 10 for a keyword. Most tools calculate KD almost entirely from the backlink profiles of the pages currently ranking — more linking domains pointing at the top results means a higher KD score. It's worth being honest about what KD does *not* measure: content quality, topical depth, or how well a page actually satisfies search intent. Treat KD as a rough filter, not a verdict — always glance at the actual top 10 results yourself before ruling a keyword out.

### Cost Per Click (CPC)

The average amount advertisers pay per click when bidding on that keyword in Google Ads. Even if you have zero interest in running paid ads, CPC is genuinely useful for organic keyword research: it's a direct signal of *commercial value*. A keyword with a $12 CPC tells you advertisers believe that traffic converts into real money — which means ranking for it organically, for free, carries real financial upside. A keyword with a $0.05 CPC is telling you the opposite.

### Traffic Potential

Covered in full detail in its own section below — but in short, this metric estimates the *total* traffic a page could earn from ranking well, accounting for every related keyword variation it could also rank for, not just the one seed keyword you searched.

### Business Potential Score

Also covered in depth below with a reference table — this score reflects how directly a keyword connects to what *you specifically* sell, separate from how many people search for it.

### Search Trend (Growth)

Most keyword tools display a small trend indicator alongside volume — showing whether interest in a keyword is rising, flat, or declining over recent months and years. A keyword with modest current volume but a clear upward trend line is frequently a better long-term bet than a keyword with higher current volume that's been steadily declining. This is especially relevant right now, since AI-driven search behavior is actively reshaping which query types are growing and which are shrinking.

### SERP Features & Click Potential

Search volume and actual clicks are no longer the same thing. In 2026, a large and growing share of Google searches — current estimates put it around 58–60% — end in **zero clicks**, because an AI Overview, featured snippet, or knowledge panel already answered the question directly on the results page. Before committing to a keyword, it's worth checking what currently occupies its search results page: if it's dominated by an AI Overview, a shopping carousel, or a featured snippet that fully answers the query, the realistic traffic ceiling is lower than the raw search volume number suggests, no matter how high that number looks.

---

## Traffic Potential {#traffic-potential}

Search volume tells you how many people search for *one specific phrase*. Traffic Potential answers a more useful question: **how much total organic traffic could this page realistically earn once it ranks well** — accounting for the fact that a single well-optimized page usually ranks for dozens, sometimes hundreds, of related keyword variations, not just the one you typed into the research tool.

Here's why this distinction matters. Imagine a keyword with 200 monthly searches. Look unimpressive on its own. But if the pages currently ranking #1 for that keyword are *also* pulling in traffic from 80 other related search terms — synonyms, plurals, question variations, related subtopics — their combined organic traffic might be closer to 4,000 monthly visits. Judging that opportunity by the 200-search "seed" keyword alone would massively undersell it.

**How to check it in practice:** Look up the page currently ranking #1 for your target keyword in a keyword research tool, and check its estimated total organic traffic (not just its ranking position for your one keyword). That total is a far more honest picture of the opportunity than the seed keyword's volume alone — and it's exactly the gap this metric was built to close, since relying on a single keyword's volume to estimate traffic potential was, in the industry's own words, a long-standing "blunder" that better data has since corrected.

**The practical takeaway:** don't dismiss a keyword just because its own search volume looks small. Check what the current top-ranking page actually earns in total traffic — that number is what you're really competing for.

---

## "Zero-Volume" Keywords: The Hidden Opportunity {#zero-volume-keywords}

Here's a number worth sitting with: **92% of all keywords show fewer than 10 monthly searches**, and a large share of those register in keyword tools as flat **zero**. If you filter those out automatically, you're ignoring the overwhelming majority of everything people actually type into Google.

### Why Tools Show "Zero" When Real People Are Searching

Keyword volume isn't measured with perfect precision — it's modeled and sampled, and tools round very small, rare numbers down to zero rather than showing an unreliable "3" or "7." A query might get searched consistently, just not often enough, or not consistently enough month to month, for the tool's model to register it confidently. Newer queries, highly specific niche phrasing, and long conversational questions are especially likely to get flagged as zero, simply because the tool hasn't accumulated enough data on that exact phrasing yet.

This effect has gotten more pronounced, not less, as search behavior shifts toward natural, conversational phrasing — voice and AI-assistant queries average around 29 words, compared to just 3–4 words for a typical typed search, and long, highly specific phrasing like that is exactly what volume tools most often under-report.

### Why "Zero" Doesn't Mean "Not Worth It"

A single zero-volume keyword won't move the needle. Dozens or hundreds of them, targeted consistently across a site, absolutely can — and individually, they tend to convert far better than head terms, precisely because the person searching that specific phrase knows exactly what they want. The chart below illustrates the shape of this: a small number of head terms carry enormous individual volume, while a vast, flat "long tail" of low- and zero-volume terms extends far beyond them — and that tail, in aggregate, is where most real search demand actually lives.

![The search demand curve showing how a small number of head keywords carry high volume while the long tail of zero-volume keywords extends far beyond them](https://smartgentools.com/blog-posts/images/keyword-research-zero-volume-demand-curve.svg)

### How to Actually Use Zero-Volume Keywords

Don't chase them as standalone targets — build them into topically comprehensive content instead. If you're writing a thorough, well-structured page around a real topic, you will naturally end up ranking for dozens of zero-volume variations of that topic without ever having deliberately targeted a single one of them by name. This is especially true for niche B2B and highly specific technical topics, where a handful of precisely-matched searchers is frequently worth more than thousands of generic visitors who never convert.

---

## Long-Tail Keywords {#long-tail-keywords}

If zero-volume keywords are the extreme tail, long-tail keywords are the broader category they belong to — and they deserve deliberate strategic attention, not just leftover scraps.

### What Makes a Keyword "Long-Tail"

Generally three or more words, highly specific, and narrowly focused on exactly one need. "Shoes" is head. "Running shoes" is mid-tail. "Best running shoes for flat feet marathon training" is long-tail — and it's also almost self-evidently transactional: whoever types that is close to buying.

### Why Long-Tail Keywords Matter More Than Their Volume Suggests

Individually, a long-tail keyword might only bring in a handful of visits a month. Collectively, they're doing most of the real work. Long-tail keywords are estimated to drive around **70% of all search traffic**, and they convert dramatically better than generic terms — long-tail traffic converts at roughly **36% on average**, compared to about **11.45%** for a typical landing page targeting a broad, generic keyword. The chart below shows this trade-off at a glance.

![Bar chart comparing long-tail versus head keywords across share of search queries, average conversion rate, and typical ranking difficulty](https://smartgentools.com/blog-posts/images/keyword-research-long-tail-vs-head-comparison.svg)

### Why This Matters Especially for Newer Sites

Competing head-on for "running shoes" against established retailers with years of backlinks is not a realistic starting strategy for a new site. Competing for "best running shoes for flat feet marathon training" is. Long-tail keywords are, in practice, the on-ramp that lets smaller or newer sites start earning real, qualified organic traffic long before they have the domain authority to compete for head terms — and once you've researched the right long-tail phrase, the natural next step is putting it to work correctly in your content and HTML, which is exactly what our [On-Page SEO Optimization guide](https://smartgentools.com/blog/on-page-seo-optimization-the-complete-a-to-z-mega-guide-for-beginners-smartgen-blog/) walks through step by step.

---

## Business Potential Score {#business-potential-score}

Search volume, traffic potential, and KD all describe a keyword from the outside — how many people search it, and how hard it is to rank for. None of them answer the one question that actually matters most for your bottom line: **if you ranked #1 for this keyword tomorrow, could you realistically turn that visitor into a customer?**

That's what the Business Potential score measures — a simple 0 to 3 scale rating how naturally your specific product or service fits into content covering that keyword. It's entirely relative to your own business: the exact same keyword can score a 3 for one company and a 0 for a direct competitor selling something adjacent but different.

| Score | What It Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **3** | Content on this keyword lets you feature your product as the direct, obvious solution. | A site selling AeroPress accessories writing about "AeroPress filters" |
| **2** | Your product is a genuinely good fit, but the connection takes a little more framing to make. | A project-management SaaS tool writing about "how to run a remote standup meeting" |
| **1** | You can mention your product in passing, but it isn't the natural focus of the content. | A CRM company writing about "how to write a professional email" |
| **0** | There's no natural way to feature your product at all, even if the topic is loosely related. | An AeroPress accessories store writing about "best thermos for coffee" |

As a general rule, prioritize keywords scoring **2 or 3** — these are the ones most likely to actually generate leads or sales, not just traffic. It's a well-tested filter: one detailed industry analysis found that roughly 77% of a company's own highest-performing content scored a 2 or 3 on exactly this scale.

---

## High-Volume Keywords: When and How to Target Them {#high-volume-keywords}

High search volume keywords aren't wrong to target — they're just a different kind of investment than long-tail keywords, with a different risk profile.

**Characteristics:** Broad, competitive, usually short-tail, and almost always backed by pages with substantial backlink profiles already occupying the top results.

**The trade-off:** High reward if you win, but a long timeline and heavy resource requirement to get there. Ranking for a high-volume head term typically demands significant content depth, strong topical authority across many related pages, and — critically — a substantial number of quality backlinks pointing at the page, which take real time to earn.

**When they make sense:** Cornerstone or pillar pages meant to anchor an entire content cluster, brand-authority content, and situations where you already have some domain strength to work with. They rarely make sense as the *first* content a brand-new site publishes, simply because the site has no existing authority to compete with what's already ranking.

**A practical middle ground:** many successful content strategies deliberately mix both — long-tail content for near-term, achievable traffic and conversions, alongside a smaller number of high-volume target pages built for the long run. Neither one alone is a complete strategy.

---

## How to Prioritize Keywords {#how-to-prioritize-keywords}

With six-plus metrics and multiple keyword types in play, prioritization is where keyword research actually turns into a plan. A workable framework combines four questions for every keyword on your list: How much total traffic is realistically available (Traffic Potential)? How directly does it connect to what you sell (Business Potential)? How hard will it be to rank for (KD)? And how much is that traffic actually worth (CPC)?

Beyond that baseline framework, two specific, slightly counterintuitive strategies are worth calling out on their own.

### Target High-KD Keywords Sooner, Not Later {#high-kd-sooner}

The instinct for most beginners is to avoid high-KD keywords entirely until the site is "strong enough." That instinct is usually backwards. High-KD keywords need a large number of backlinks to rank — and earning those backlinks takes real time, often many months, regardless of when you start. If you wait until your site feels "ready" before publishing on a competitive topic, you're simply delaying the point at which that content-and-backlink clock even starts ticking. Publishing genuinely strong content on a hard keyword today, then building links to it steadily over the following months, almost always beats waiting a year and starting the same process from scratch later.

### Use High-KD Keywords as Link-Building Opportunities {#high-kd-link-opportunities}

There's a second, less obvious reason high-KD topics are worth attention early: competitive, high-KD topics are usually competitive precisely *because* they're genuinely valuable, widely-discussed subjects — which also makes them naturally more link-worthy. A truly comprehensive, well-researched resource on a hard, high-value topic is far more likely to earn natural backlinks from other sites than a thin page on an obscure long-tail phrase nobody else is writing about. In that sense, a handful of ambitious high-KD pages can function as **linkable assets** — content specifically built to attract external links — which then strengthens the authority of your entire site, not just that one page. For the full playbook on actually earning those links once the content exists, see our [Off-Page Optimization guide](https://smartgentools.com/blog/off-page-optimization-the-complete-a-to-z-mega-guide-for-beginners-smartgen-blog/).

### Use CPC as a Commercial Value Tiebreaker

When two keywords look similar on volume, KD, and business potential, CPC is a clean tiebreaker. Higher CPC signals real advertiser demand and, by extension, real monetary value behind that search intent — a strong reason to prioritize it over a similarly-scored keyword with a near-zero CPC.

---

## Step-by-Step Keyword Research Process {#step-by-step-process}

Bringing everything above together, here's a practical workflow to follow from a blank page to a prioritized keyword list ready to turn into content.

**Step 1 — Brainstorm seed keywords.** List 10–20 broad topics genuinely related to your business, products, or services. Don't filter yet — just capture the territory.

**Step 2 — Expand each seed into a full keyword list.** Run each seed through a keyword research tool to surface related terms, questions, and long-tail variations. Most tools organize these into topic groups and subgroups, which makes it far faster to spot clusters than scrolling one long flat list.

**Step 3 — Pull the core metrics for every keyword.** Search Volume, KD, CPC, and Traffic Potential for the top-ranking page, at minimum.

**Step 4 — Score Business Potential.** Go through the list and rate each keyword 0–3 using the table above. This step alone eliminates a large share of technically-high-volume keywords that would never realistically convert for your business.

**Step 5 — Check search intent by actually looking at the SERP.** For any keyword you're seriously considering, search it and look at what's currently ranking — and what's occupying the page above the organic results. If AI Overviews or a featured snippet already fully answer the query, or if the top 10 are dominated by a content type you can't realistically match (video, product listings, forums), that's a signal to adjust your target or your content format.

**Step 6 — Prioritize using the combined framework.** Favor keywords with strong Business Potential (2–3), reasonable Traffic Potential, and a KD your site can realistically compete for right now — while still reserving a portion of your roadmap for ambitious, high-KD linkable-asset content, per the strategy above.

**Step 7 — Map keywords to content, not the other way around.** Group related keywords into single, comprehensive pages rather than writing a separate thin page for every keyword variation — this is also how you naturally capture the zero-volume long tail without targeting it directly. Our [Content Marketing guide](https://smartgentools.com/blog/content-marketing-the-complete-a-to-z-mega-guide-for-beginners-smartgen-blog/) covers how to plan and structure that content at scale.

**Step 8 — Write titles and descriptions that reflect the actual keyword, then verify the snippet.** Once the keyword is chosen, check how your title and meta description will actually appear in search results before publishing — our free [SERP Preview Tool](https://smartgentools.com/serp-preview-tool/) shows exactly this, so nothing gets cut off or misrepresented in the results page.

**Step 9 — Write naturally, then verify keyword usage.** Once a first draft is done, run it through a [Keyword Density Checker](https://smartgentools.com/keyword-density-checker/) to confirm your target keyword appears often enough to be clearly relevant, without tipping into stuffing.

**Step 10 — Track and refine.** Keyword research isn't a one-time task. Revisit your priority list every few months — search trends shift, new competitors enter the SERP, and keywords that looked unrealistic six months ago may now be within reach.

---

## Visual Summary

The infographic below brings the full framework together — keyword metrics, the prioritization matrix, and the Business Potential scale, in one reference view.

![Keyword research framework infographic showing the seven core metrics, a prioritization matrix, and the Business Potential scale](https://smartgentools.com/blog-posts/images/keyword-research-framework-infographic.svg)

---

## Frequently Asked Questions {#faq}

**How many keywords should I target on a single page?**
One primary keyword per page, supported by as many closely related variations and long-tail phrases as fit naturally into comprehensive coverage of the topic. Trying to force multiple, distinct primary keywords onto one page usually dilutes its relevance for all of them rather than strengthening any single one.

**What's a realistic KD range for a brand-new website?**
There's no universal number, since it depends heavily on your niche's overall competitiveness — but as a general starting point, many new sites find early traction in the low-to-mid KD range while reserving very high-KD topics for later, better-linked pages, alongside the "sooner, not later" strategy described above for a select few ambitious targets.

**Should I ignore zero-volume keywords completely?**
No — but don't treat them as standalone targets either. Build comprehensive content around real topics, and you'll pick up dozens of zero-volume variations automatically without ever having to research them individually by name.

**Is search volume or Traffic Potential more important?**
Traffic Potential, in most cases — it reflects the realistic total opportunity of a topic rather than one narrow phrase's isolated number, and it's far less likely to make you dismiss a genuinely valuable topic because its seed keyword happened to look small.

**If I don't run paid ads, does CPC still matter?**
Yes. CPC is one of the clearest available signals of commercial intent and monetary value behind a search term, entirely independent of whether you personally advertise. High CPC on a keyword you can rank for organically is effectively free access to traffic advertisers are actively paying for.

**Can a keyword have high Business Potential but low search volume?**
Absolutely, and these are often some of the best keywords available — highly specific, highly relevant to exactly what you sell, and comparatively easy to rank for precisely because fewer competitors bother targeting them.

**How often should I redo keyword research?**
Revisit your core keyword list every few months at minimum, and any time you notice a meaningful shift in your traffic, your niche, or your competitors' content. Search behavior — especially with AI-driven search growing — is changing faster now than it has in years.

**How has AI search changed keyword research in 2026?**
Search behavior is shifting toward longer, more conversational, question-style queries rather than short two- or three-word phrases, and a growing share of searches are answered directly on the results page without a click at all. The practical response isn't to abandon keyword research — it's to focus more on building genuinely comprehensive, authoritative content around real topics, since that approach naturally captures both the traditional keyword and its many conversational, zero-volume variants at once.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Keywords come in several overlapping types — short-tail, long-tail, informational, navigational, commercial, transactional, branded, and local — and knowing which type you're looking at shapes what content format actually fits.
- Search Volume, KD, CPC, Traffic Potential, Business Potential, Search Trend, and SERP Features together give a complete picture — no single metric should drive a decision alone.
- "Zero volume" is frequently a data limitation, not a real absence of demand — long-tail and zero-volume terms collectively make up the majority of all search traffic.
- The Business Potential score (0–3) is the fastest way to filter out keywords that would bring traffic but never convert.
- High-KD keywords are worth starting on early, not avoiding — both because ranking takes time regardless of when you start, and because they can function as link-attracting assets for your whole site.

# pyproject.toml Guide: Write, Configure & Fix Common Errors (2026)

If you have ever opened a Python repository and found `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `requirements.txt`, and a half-finished `MANIFEST.in` all fighting for control of the same project, you already know why `pyproject.toml` exists. It replaces that pile of files with a single, readable configuration file that every modern Python tool — pip, build, Hatch, Poetry, uv, linters, type checkers — knows how to read.

This guide walks through the whole thing end to end: what each field actually does, a full working example you can copy, a step-by-step walkthrough for starting from zero, a migration path from `setup.py`, and — because this is where almost everyone gets stuck — a dedicated troubleshooting section that explains *why* the most common errors happen and exactly how to fix them. It also covers something a lot of 2024- and 2025-era tutorials still get wrong: the `license` field's format changed under **PEP 639**, and the old syntax now throws a build error on current tooling. That gets its own section below.

## Quick Answer

The smallest working `pyproject.toml` needs just two tables:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "your-package-name"
version = "0.1.0"
```

`[build-system]` tells installers *which tool* turns your source code into an installable package. `[project]` holds the metadata — name, version, dependencies, and so on — that almost every tool reads the same way. A third table, `[tool]`, holds settings specific to individual tools like Ruff, Black, or pytest, and isn't standardized at all. Everything below explains how to fill these in properly, field by field, plus the mistakes that break each one.

## What Is pyproject.toml, and Why Did It Replace setup.py?

For most of Python's packaging history, project metadata lived inside `setup.py` — a file that had to be *executed* before a tool could even find out your package's name or dependencies. That created a real problem: to learn what your project needed to build itself, pip first had to run arbitrary Python code, which meant the build environment already had to have the right dependencies installed just to discover what dependencies it needed. It was slow, inconsistent across machines, and quietly insecure, since installing a package could mean running someone else's code before you'd agreed to anything.

Two Python Enhancement Proposals fixed this in stages. **PEP 518** (2017) introduced `pyproject.toml` itself, solving the immediate problem by giving tools a static, declarative place — the `[build-system]` table — to list what's needed *before* any code runs. **PEP 621** (2020) went further and standardized general project metadata (name, dependencies, authors, and so on) into the `[project]` table, so that metadata could finally be read the same way regardless of which build tool a project used.

`setup.py` isn't strictly forbidden today — it's still valid, and some projects keep a slimmed-down version around for genuinely programmatic needs, like compiling a C extension with logic that can't be expressed declaratively. But for a new project, there's no longer a reason to start there. The `[project]` table covers the vast majority of what `setup()` used to do, without needing to execute anything.

TOML itself (Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language) is the format doing the heavy lifting here. It reads like a slightly stricter INI file — sections in square brackets, `key = value` pairs, native support for strings, arrays, and nested tables — and it's the same format Rust's Cargo uses for `Cargo.toml`, which is part of why it was chosen: predictable, boring, and easy to parse without ambiguity.

## The Three Tables Inside Every pyproject.toml

| Table | Required? | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `[build-system]` | Strongly recommended for every project | Declares which build backend turns your source into a wheel/sdist, and what's needed to run it |
| `[project]` | Used by most backends | Your project's metadata: name, version, dependencies, description, and so on |
| `[tool]` | Optional, per-tool | Tool-specific settings, e.g. `[tool.ruff]`, `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`. Format is defined entirely by each tool |

One exception worth knowing about: **Poetry**, before version 2.0 (released January 2025), didn't use `[project]` at all — it kept everything under `[tool.poetry]` instead. Poetry 2.0+ supports both, but if you're reading an older Poetry project, that's why the metadata looks like it's in the "wrong" place.

## Step 1: Choose and Declare Your Build Backend — `[build-system]`

The build backend is the program that actually turns your source files into a distributable package (a wheel and/or source distribution). `[build-system]` has two keys: `build-backend`, which names it, and `requires`, a list of what needs to be installed to run it — typically just the backend itself, sometimes with a version floor.

You'll generally copy this straight from whichever backend's documentation, but here's what the current versions look like for the most common options:

| Backend | `requires` | `build-backend` | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hatchling** | `"hatchling>=1.26"` | `"hatchling.build"` | New projects wanting sensible defaults with minimal config |
| **setuptools** | `"setuptools>=77.0.3"` | `"setuptools.build_meta"` | Existing projects, C extensions, the most battle-tested option |
| **Flit** | `"flit_core>=3.12,<4"` | `"flit_core.buildapi"` | Simple pure-Python packages, minimal configuration |
| **PDM** | `"pdm-backend>=2.4.0"` | `"pdm.backend"` | Projects already using PDM for dependency management |
| **uv-build** | `"uv_build>=0.11.23,<0.12.0"` | `"uv_build"` | Projects already using uv, fastest install/build step |
| **Poetry-core** | `"poetry-core>=2.2.0"` | `"poetry.core.masonry.api"` | Projects using Poetry for dependency locking |

For a caching library called `quickcache`, using Hatchling, that section looks like this:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling>=1.26"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"
```

None of these are objectively "correct" — they all produce a standard wheel that pip can install. If you don't already have a preference, Hatchling is a reasonable default for a new pure-Python project: minimal configuration, sensible defaults, and current SPDX license support (more on why that matters shortly).

## Step 2: Static vs. Dynamic Metadata

Most `[project]` fields are just written directly: `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, `version = "1.2.0"`. But sometimes you don't want to hardcode a value — the most common case is version numbers, which people often want to read from a `__version__` variable in their code or from a Git tag, rather than typing the number twice.

For that, mark the field as `dynamic`, and let the build backend fill it in at build time:

```toml
[project]
dynamic = ["version"]
```

The exact mechanism for *how* a dynamic field gets its value depends entirely on your backend's own configuration — for Hatchling, for example, you'd add a `[tool.hatch.version]` table pointing at the source. The one field that can never be dynamic is `name`, since tools need it to even know what project they're looking at.

## Step 3: The Required Basics — `name` and `version`

```toml
[project]
name = "quickcache"
version = "0.1.0"
```

`name` is the only field that's both required and can never be dynamic. It's also more restrictive than it looks: it must be made of ASCII letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, and periods, and it can't start or end with an underscore, hyphen, or period. Comparisons are case-insensitive, and runs of `_`, `-`, and `.` are treated as interchangeable — so `Quick-Cache`, `quick.cache`, and `QUICK__cache` all resolve to the same registered project on PyPI. This is exactly the rule that trips people up when a name has spaces or symbols in it (more in the mistakes section below).

`version` is technically required too, but in practice it's one of the most commonly *dynamic* fields, for the reason above — most people don't want to hand-edit a version number in two places every release.

## Step 4: Declare Your Dependencies

### requires-python

```toml
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.9"
```

This declares the minimum Python version your project supports. One thing worth knowing: resist the urge to add an *upper* bound here, like `requires-python = ">=3.9,<3.13"`. It feels safe, but it tends to actively break things — it prevents your package from being installed at all on Python versions that come out after you publish, even if your code would have worked fine on them. Pin upper bounds on individual dependencies if you must, not on Python itself.

### dependencies

```toml
[project]
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.27",
    "click>=8.1",
    "colorama>=0.4; sys_platform == 'win32'",
]
```

Each string is a standard dependency specifier: package name, optional version constraints, and optionally an environment marker after a semicolon — the `colorama` line above only installs on Windows, for example. Everything in this list gets installed automatically whenever someone runs `pip install quickcache`, so this is only for things every user of your package genuinely needs.

### optional-dependencies (extras)

```toml
[project.optional-dependencies]
redis = ["redis>=5.0"]
cli = ["rich>=13.0", "click>=8.1"]
dev = ["pytest>=8.0", "mypy>=1.10"]
```

Each key here defines a named "extra." Someone who only needs the Redis backend installs it with `pip install quickcache[redis]`, which pulls in the base package plus whatever's listed under that key. This is the right tool when a dependency is only needed for *one feature* of your package — not for general development tooling, which brings us to the next section.

## Step 5: Separate Dev Dependencies With `[dependency-groups]`

This is the newest piece of the standard, and it's worth understanding even though it's optional, because it solves a real, long-standing mess.

Before this existed, every tool invented its own private spot for "dependencies you need to develop the project, but that shouldn't ship to your users" — pytest, mypy, sphinx, and so on. Poetry used `[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies]`. PDM used `[tool.pdm.dev-dependencies]`. Early uv used `[tool.uv.dev-dependencies]`. None of them could read each other's tables, so switching tools meant rewriting your dev dependencies from scratch.

**PEP 735** standardizes this with a new **top-level** table — not nested inside `[project]` — called `[dependency-groups]`:

```toml
[dependency-groups]
test = ["pytest>=8.0", "pytest-cov>=5.0"]
docs = ["sphinx>=7.0", "sphinx-rtd-theme"]
typing = ["mypy>=1.10", "types-redis"]
dev = [{include-group = "test"}, {include-group = "typing"}]
```

Groups can reference other groups with `{include-group = "name"}` instead of duplicating entries, which is how the `dev` group above pulls in both `test` and `typing` without repeating anything.

Tool support as of 2026: uv has full support (`uv sync --group test`, `uv add --group test pytest`), pip added a `--group` flag for installing from these tables starting in version 25.1, and Poetry reads `[dependency-groups]` from version 2.2.0 onward, with 2.3.0+ recommended for reliable lockfile behavior. The field that trips people up most: this table sits at the *top level* of the file, as its own `[dependency-groups]` heading — not as `[project.dependency-groups]`. Getting that indentation/nesting wrong is a quiet, common mistake.

## Step 6: Describe Your Project for Humans and for PyPI

```toml
[project]
description = "A lightweight, pluggable caching library for Python."
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    {name = "Jordan Kade", email = "jordan@example.com"},
]
maintainers = [
    {name = "Jordan Kade", email = "jordan@example.com"},
]
keywords = ["cache", "caching", "redis", "memoization"]
classifiers = [
    "Development Status :: 4 - Beta",
    "Intended Audience :: Developers",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.9",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.13",
]

[project.urls]
Homepage = "https://example.com/quickcache"
Documentation = "https://quickcache.readthedocs.io"
Repository = "https://github.com/example/quickcache"
Issues = "https://github.com/example/quickcache/issues"
Changelog = "https://github.com/example/quickcache/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md"
```

A few notes worth knowing:

- **`readme`** auto-detects its format from the file extension — `README.md` is treated as GitHub-flavored Markdown, `README.rst` as reStructuredText. You can override this explicitly with `readme = {file = "README.txt", content-type = "text/markdown"}` if your filename doesn't match the content.
- **`classifiers`** come from a fixed list (browsable at PyPI's classifier list) and are used for *browsing and search* on PyPI — they don't actually restrict installation. If you list `Programming Language :: Python :: 3.9`, that's informational only; `requires-python` is what actually enforces a minimum version.
- **`urls`** populates the sidebar links on your PyPI project page. Stick to recognizable labels like `Homepage`, `Repository`, `Issues`, `Documentation`, and `Changelog` where you can — PyPI recognizes a specific set of "well-known" labels and displays them with matching icons; anything else still works, just renders as plain text instead.

## Step 7: License and License Files — What Changed in 2026

This is the section most existing tutorials get wrong, because the standard changed underneath them. If you've copied a `license` example from an article written before mid-2025, there's a good chance it's now using a deprecated syntax that current build backends reject outright.

**The old, deprecated format** wrote `license` as a table:

```toml
# Deprecated (option A) — many build backends now reject this
license = {text = "MIT"}
```
```toml
# Deprecated (option B) — same problem
license = {file = "LICENSE"}
```

**The current format**, standardized by **PEP 639**, treats `license` as a plain string containing a valid SPDX license expression, and separates out the actual license file(s) into their own key:

```toml
[project]
license = "MIT"
license-files = ["LICENSE*"]
```

You can combine licenses with standard SPDX boolean syntax when a project is multi-licensed:

```toml
license = "MIT AND (Apache-2.0 OR BSD-2-Clause)"
```

And if your license doesn't have an official SPDX identifier, you can register a custom one following the `LicenseRef-` prefix convention:

```toml
license = "LicenseRef-My-Custom-License"
```

`license-files` takes a list of **glob patterns**, not a single fixed filename, which is genuinely useful if you vendor third-party licenses alongside your own:

```toml
license-files = ["LICEN[CS]E*", "vendored/licenses/*.txt", "AUTHORS.md"]
```

Here's the practical part: build backends had to explicitly add support for this new format, and if yours predates that, you'll get a build error saying `license` should be a table/dict — which is backwards from what you'd expect, since the table format is the *old* one. That error means your backend version is too old, not that your syntax is wrong. Minimum versions that support the new PEP 639 format:

| hatchling | setuptools | flit-core | pdm-backend | poetry-core | uv-build |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.27.0 | 77.0.3 | 3.12 | 2.4.0 | 2.2.0 | 0.7.19 |

If you're on an older pin, bumping the version in `[build-system] requires` is usually the entire fix.

## Step 8: Add Console Scripts, GUI Scripts, and Plugins

If you want `pip install quickcache` to also drop a command into the user's terminal, declare it under `[project.scripts]`:

```toml
[project.scripts]
quickcache-cli = "quickcache.cli:main"
```

This installs a `quickcache-cli` command that's the equivalent of running `import sys; from quickcache.cli import main; sys.exit(main())`. If your entry point launches a GUI instead of a terminal tool, use `[project.gui-scripts]` instead — on Windows, this is the difference between your app quietly opening a window versus popping up an unwanted console behind it. On other platforms the two behave identically.

For a plugin system — letting other packages register themselves into yours, the way pytest and Pygments plugins work — use `[project.entry-points]` with a custom group name:

```toml
[project.entry-points."quickcache.backends"]
memory = "quickcache.backends.memory:MemoryBackend"
redis = "quickcache.backends.redis:RedisBackend"
```

Your own code can then discover whatever's registered under `"quickcache.backends"` at runtime via `importlib.metadata.entry_points()`, without needing to know in advance what plugins exist.

## Full Example: Every Field Working Together

Here's everything above combined into one coherent, copyable file:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling>=1.26"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "quickcache"
dynamic = ["version"]
description = "A lightweight, pluggable caching library for Python."
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.9"
license = "MIT"
license-files = ["LICENSE*"]
authors = [
    {name = "Jordan Kade", email = "jordan@example.com"},
]
maintainers = [
    {name = "Jordan Kade", email = "jordan@example.com"},
]
keywords = ["cache", "caching", "redis", "memoization"]
classifiers = [
    "Development Status :: 4 - Beta",
    "Intended Audience :: Developers",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.9",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.13",
]
dependencies = [
    "click>=8.1",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
redis = ["redis>=5.0"]
cli = ["rich>=13.0"]

[dependency-groups]
test = ["pytest>=8.0", "pytest-cov>=5.0"]
typing = ["mypy>=1.10"]
dev = [{include-group = "test"}, {include-group = "typing"}]

[project.urls]
Homepage = "https://example.com/quickcache"
Repository = "https://github.com/example/quickcache"
Issues = "https://github.com/example/quickcache/issues"

[project.scripts]
quickcache-cli = "quickcache.cli:main"

[project.entry-points."quickcache.backends"]
memory = "quickcache.backends.memory:MemoryBackend"
redis = "quickcache.backends.redis:RedisBackend"

[tool.hatch.version]
path = "src/quickcache/__init__.py"
```

## Build Your First pyproject.toml From Scratch (Step-by-Step)

If you're starting a brand-new project, here's the whole path from an empty folder to an installable package.

1. **Create the project structure.** A "src layout" — putting your package inside a `src/` folder — is worth adopting even for small projects, because it prevents Python from accidentally importing your uninstalled source code instead of the properly installed package during testing:
   ```
   quickcache/
   ├── src/
   │   └── quickcache/
   │       ├── __init__.py
   │       └── cli.py
   ├── tests/
   ├── pyproject.toml
   └── README.md
   ```

2. **Write a minimal `pyproject.toml`** at the root:
   ```toml
   [build-system]
   requires = ["hatchling>=1.26"]
   build-backend = "hatchling.build"

   [project]
   name = "quickcache"
   version = "0.1.0"
   description = "A lightweight caching library."
   requires-python = ">=3.9"
   ```

3. **Create and activate a virtual environment**, so you're not installing anything system-wide:
   ```bash
   python -m venv .venv
   source .venv/bin/activate   # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
   ```

4. **Install the `build` package**, which is the standard PyPA tool for producing distributions:
   ```bash
   pip install build
   ```

5. **Build it**:
   ```bash
   python -m build
   ```
   This creates a `dist/` folder containing both a wheel (`.whl`) and a source distribution (`.tar.gz`).

6. **Install it locally in editable mode** while you're developing, so code changes show up immediately without rebuilding:
   ```bash
   pip install -e .
   ```

7. **Confirm it imports correctly**:
   ```bash
   python -c "import quickcache; print(quickcache.__file__)"
   ```

From here, everything else — dependencies, entry points, classifiers — is just adding more fields to the `[project]` table you already have.

## Migrating an Existing setup.py Project (Step-by-Step)

If you're modernizing an older project rather than starting fresh, the mapping from `setup()` keyword arguments to `[project]` fields is mostly one-to-one:

| Old (`setup.py` argument) | New (`pyproject.toml` field) |
|---|---|
| `name=` | `name` |
| `version=` | `version` (or `dynamic = ["version"]`) |
| `install_requires=` | `dependencies` |
| `extras_require=` | `[project.optional-dependencies]` |
| `python_requires=` | `requires-python` |
| `author=`, `author_email=` | `authors = [{name=..., email=...}]` |
| `long_description=` | `readme` |
| `url=` | `[project.urls] Homepage = ...` |
| `classifiers=` | `classifiers` |
| `entry_points={"console_scripts": [...]}` | `[project.scripts]` |

Practical steps:

1. **Add a `[build-system]` table first**, even before touching anything else. Just its presence — even in an otherwise empty `pyproject.toml` — changes pip's default behavior to build your project in an isolated environment, which is itself a meaningful reliability improvement:
   ```toml
   [build-system]
   requires = ["setuptools>=77.0.3"]
   build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"
   ```
2. **Copy your metadata across** using the mapping table above.
3. **Decide whether `setup.py` still needs to exist.** It's completely valid for it to remain if you have genuinely programmatic build logic — compiling a C extension, for instance. If your `setup.py` only ever called `setup()` with static keyword arguments, you can delete it once everything's been moved.
4. **Keep `MANIFEST.in`** only if you're bundling non-Python files into your source distribution that need custom inclusion rules; it still works alongside `pyproject.toml`.
5. **Rebuild and compare.** Run `python -m build` and check that the file listing inside the new wheel/sdist matches what the old setup produced — `unzip -l dist/*.whl` is a quick way to eyeball it.

## Validate Your File Before You Publish

Three checks, cheapest first:

**1. Confirm it's valid TOML at all**, using Python's built-in parser (3.11+; use the `tomli` package on older versions):
```bash
python -c "import tomllib; print(tomllib.load(open('pyproject.toml', 'rb')))"
```
If this throws an error, you have a syntax problem — a stray quote, a duplicate table, bad indentation — before you even get to whether the *content* is valid.

**2. Check it against the packaging specification itself** with [validate-pyproject](https://pypi.org/project/validate-pyproject/), a dedicated schema-based validator that checks compliance with PEP 517, 518, 621, 639, and 735 in one pass:
```bash
pip install validate-pyproject
validate-pyproject pyproject.toml
```
It can also run as a pre-commit hook, so this check happens automatically before every commit rather than only when you remember to run it manually.

**3. Do a real build as a smoke test.** A broken `pyproject.toml` will usually fail immediately here, with a much clearer error than pip gives you downstream:
```bash
python -m build --sdist
```

## 12 Common pyproject.toml Mistakes (and Exactly How to Fix Each One)

These are drawn from real, recurring issues across pip, uv, Poetry, and setuptools — not hypothetical ones.

### 1. Missing the `[build-system]` table entirely
**Symptom:** Inconsistent build behavior, or tools falling back to legacy assumptions you didn't intend.
**Fix:** Add it, even if you add nothing else:
```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling>=1.26"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"
```

### 2. An invalid project name
**Symptom:** An error like `Not a valid package or extra name`, often triggered by a name with a space or symbol in it, e.g. `name = "my cool package"`.
**Fix:** Use only letters, digits, hyphens, underscores, and periods, and don't start or end with a separator:
```toml
name = "my-cool-package"
```

### 3. `version` is missing and not marked dynamic
**Symptom:** A validation error complaining that required metadata is absent.
**Fix:** Either set it directly, or explicitly mark it dynamic and configure your backend to supply it:
```toml
version = "0.1.0"
# or
dynamic = ["version"]
```

### 4. A field is both static and dynamic at the same time
**Symptom:** A metadata conflict error — this happens when a field like `dependencies` has a real value *and* also appears in the `dynamic` list.
**Fix:** Pick one. If a build backend is computing it for you, remove the static value and leave only the `dynamic` entry (or vice versa).

### 5. Using the old `license = {file = "..."}` table format
**Symptom:** A build error saying `license` should be a string, not a table — on any backend version listed in the PEP 639 support table above.
**Fix:** Switch to the SPDX string format:
```toml
license = "MIT"
license-files = ["LICENSE*"]
```

### 6. `build-backend` doesn't match the package in `requires`
**Symptom:** A build backend import failure — the tool named in `build-backend` isn't actually installed, because it wasn't listed in `requires`.
**Fix:** Make sure the two agree. If you use Hatchling, both lines need to say Hatchling:
```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling>=1.26"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"
```

### 7. Dependency specifiers with bad syntax
**Symptom:** A parse error on your dependency list, often from missing quotes around a version constraint or a malformed environment marker.
**Fix:** Every dependency is a quoted string, constraint and all:
```toml
dependencies = [
    "requests>=2.31",
    "colorama>=0.4; sys_platform == 'win32'",
]
```

### 8. An overly strict `requires-python` upper bound
**Symptom:** Your package becomes uninstallable on newer Python releases the moment they come out, even though nothing about your code actually breaks.
**Fix:** Avoid upper bounds on `requires-python` specifically — use a lower bound only, and pin upper bounds on individual dependencies instead if one of *them* has a known incompatibility.

### 9. A `[project.scripts]` entry pointing at the wrong path
**Symptom:** The installed command exists but crashes immediately with an import error.
**Fix:** The value must be `"module.path:function_name"`, matching your actual source layout — with a src layout, that's relative to `src/`, not the repo root:
```toml
[project.scripts]
quickcache-cli = "quickcache.cli:main"
```

### 10. Duplicate table headers
**Symptom:** A TOML parse error, or metadata silently overwriting itself — usually the result of copy-pasting a second `[project]` block from another file during a merge.
**Fix:** Each table header can appear once. Merge the contents under a single `[project]` heading.

### 11. A `readme` path that doesn't match the real file
**Symptom:** `twine check` fails on your long description, even though the package still uploads — the check is separate from the upload step.
**Fix:** Confirm the exact filename and extension:
```toml
readme = "README.md"
```

### 12. Forgetting `license-files`
**Symptom:** Nothing crashes, but your actual `LICENSE` file never ships inside the built package, which is a real compliance gap for anyone redistributing your code.
**Fix:** Add the glob explicitly — it doesn't happen automatically just because a `LICENSE` file exists in your repo:
```toml
license-files = ["LICENSE*"]
```

## Building and Publishing Your Package (Quick Path)

Once your file validates and builds cleanly:

1. **Build both distributions:**
   ```bash
   python -m build
   ```
2. **Sanity-check the result:**
   ```bash
   pip install twine
   twine check dist/*
   ```
3. **Upload to TestPyPI first** — a separate, throwaway index made exactly for this — before touching the real one:
   ```bash
   twine upload --repository testpypi dist/*
   ```
   You'll authenticate with username `__token__` and a TestPyPI API token as the password (PyPI and TestPyPI both removed plain password auth in 2024).
4. **Install from TestPyPI to confirm it actually works** end to end:
   ```bash
   pip install --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ quickcache
   ```
5. **Publish for real** once you're satisfied:
   ```bash
   twine upload dist/*
   ```

If you'd rather automate this on every tagged release, GitHub Actions CI/CD workflows are the standard next step — worth setting up once you're publishing more than a couple of times.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do I still need setup.py?**
Not for a new project. It remains valid for cases needing genuinely programmatic build logic, like compiling C extensions, but the `[project]` table covers standard metadata without it.

**What's the actual difference between `dependencies` and `[dependency-groups]`?**
`dependencies` (and `optional-dependencies`) describe what your *published package* needs to run, and they ship with it. `[dependency-groups]` describes what *you* need to develop it — test runners, linters, docs builders — and none of it is included when someone installs your package from PyPI.

**Why does pip suddenly build my project in an isolated environment?**
Simply having a `pyproject.toml` file — even a mostly empty one — changes pip's default behavior to use build isolation, which is generally a good thing for reproducibility.

**Can `[project]` and `[tool.poetry]` coexist?**
Yes, as of Poetry 2.0+. Older Poetry projects (pre-January 2025) only used `[tool.poetry]`, which is why you'll still see that pattern in older repositories.

**Is TOML case-sensitive?**
Table and key names are case-sensitive, but the `name` field specifically is compared case-insensitively for PyPI registration purposes, along with treating runs of `-`, `_`, and `.` as equivalent.

**What Python version do I need just to read a pyproject.toml myself?**
Python 3.11+ includes `tomllib` in the standard library. For anything earlier, install the `tomli` package, which implements the same interface.

## Key Takeaways

- Every project should have a `[build-system]` table, even a minimal one — its mere presence changes how pip builds your project for the better.
- `[project]` is the standardized home for metadata; only `name` can never be dynamic.
- The `license` field's format changed under PEP 639: it's now a plain SPDX string, not a table — and this is the single most common thing outdated tutorials get wrong.
- Use `[dependency-groups]` (a top-level table) for development-only dependencies, and `[project.optional-dependencies]` for features your users can opt into.
- Validate before you publish: `tomllib` for syntax, `validate-pyproject` for spec compliance, and a real `python -m build` as a final smoke test.
- Always push to TestPyPI before the real index — it exists specifically so a mistake doesn't cost you a package name or version number on the real one.

## Further Reading


- [PyPA: Writing your pyproject.toml](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/writing-pyproject-toml/) — the canonical technical reference this guide is built on top of
- [PyPA: How to modernize a setup.py based project](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/modernize-setup-py-project/)
- [PyPA: Using TestPyPI](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/using-testpypi/)
- [PEP 621 – Storing project metadata in pyproject.toml](https://peps.python.org/pep-0621/)
- [PEP 639 – Improving License Clarity with Better Package Metadata](https://peps.python.org/pep-0639/)
- [PEP 735 – Dependency Groups in pyproject.toml](https://peps.python.org/pep-0735/)
- [validate-pyproject on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/validate-pyproject/)
- [build on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/build/)
- [twine on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/twine/)
